title_ref: Causal Machine Learning Is Not a Panacea: A Roadmap for Observational Causal Inference in Health
notes: Claim/reasoning graph constructed in the same schema as the DecomposeRL example graph. This source document (a JAMIA-style perspective/roadmap article, not a preprint with an arXiv ID) was not pre-segmented with sentence IDs, so evidence tags (E1, E2, ...) are paraphrase-anchored references to specific statements in the provided text rather than exact sentence indices.

components.description: Motivation: why causal ML on observational data is attractive, and why that attractiveness creates risk.

nodes.name: RCTs not always feasible
nodes.description: Randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard for establishing causal relationships, but are not always feasible due to ethical or logistical constraints.

nodes.name: Observational data seen as a bridge
nodes.description: Researchers may consider causal inference on large-scale observational, retrospective data as a bridge between gold-standard RCTs and ubiquitous real-world data.

nodes.name: Curated observational data can emulate an RCT
nodes.description: When observational data are curated to follow a set of assumptions, causal inference can be applied to emulate an RCT, yielding valid treatment effect estimates.

nodes.name: Causal ML promising for complex confounders
nodes.description: Causal ML shows promise because ML excels at extracting signals from multi-modal data (images, notes, time-series), allowing adjustment on complex confounders that traditional statistical methods struggle to incorporate.

nodes.name: ML flexibility increases risk of erroneous findings
nodes.description: Drawing valid causal inferences requires justifying assumptions in the data and modeling choices; the flexibility of ML increases the risk of erroneous findings.

nodes.name: Erroneous causal conclusions risk patient safety
nodes.description: Inappropriately drawing causal conclusions from ML carries risks to medical science and potentially patient safety.

nodes.name: Limitations of causal ML under-appreciated
nodes.description: Despite advances in causal ML, its limitations remain largely under-appreciated across disciplines, and this gap in shared knowledge may impact the validity of findings.

components.description: Causal DAG as the foundation for identifiability, and how ML's optimization for prediction creates new verification challenges.

nodes.name: Non-random treatment assignment causes confounding
nodes.description: When estimating causal effects from observational data, treatments are often non-randomly assigned, confounding direct comparisons of outcomes.

nodes.name: Causal DAG models treatment-outcome relationships
nodes.description: The causal relationships between treatment, outcome, and other relevant variables can be modeled using a causal directed acyclic graph (DAG).

nodes.name: DAG structure implies identifiability assumptions
nodes.description: The structure of a causal DAG implies a set of independence conditions between variables that generate identifiability assumptions, determining when a causal interpretation of treatment effects is tenable.

nodes.name: Accurate DAG construction is a crucial first step
nodes.description: Constructing an accurate DAG with input from domain experts is a crucial first step in ensuring meaningful causal conclusions.

nodes.name: ML models optimized for prediction, not causal validity
nodes.description: By default, most ML approaches are optimized for predictive performance.

nodes.name: ML may exploit spurious associations
nodes.description: Because ML is optimized for predictive performance, ML models may leverage spurious associations to make predictions even when an underlying causal relationship exists.

nodes.name: This obscures identifiability-assumption violations
nodes.description: This tendency to exploit spurious associations means ML introduces new challenges in verifying (and can obscure violations of) the causal identifiability assumptions.

components.description: The Overlap assumption: how to assess it, and the diagnostic ambiguity of propensity-model performance.

nodes.name: Overlap assumption defined
nodes.description: The overlap assumption requires every patient to have a non-zero probability of receiving the treatment.

nodes.name: Propensity model used to assess overlap
nodes.description: Overlap can be partly assessed by fitting a propensity score model to predict treatment assignment from variables that could influence it, per the causal DAG.

nodes.name: High discrimination + well-specified model implies low overlap
nodes.description: If the propensity model is well-specified, high discriminative performance implies low overlap, while poor discriminative performance indicates more randomness in treatment assignment.

nodes.name: Poor performance can also indicate underfitting
nodes.description: If the model is poorly specified, near-random discriminative performance could simply indicate underfitting rather than true overlap.

nodes.name: Standard ML techniques mitigate specification issues
nodes.description: Issues with model specification can be mitigated in part using standard supervised ML techniques such as cross-validation for model selection.

nodes.name: Domain experts needed for thorough overlap evaluation
nodes.description: To more thoroughly evaluate overlap, one should consult domain experts, ideally those responsible for assigning the treatments, who can help identify settings where overlap is impossible.

components.description: Conditional exchangeability (no unobserved confounding): unverifiability and mitigation strategies.

nodes.name: No-unobserved-confounding is unverifiable
nodes.description: The assumption of no unobserved confounding is unverifiable in observational data.

nodes.name: Identifying confounders requires domain expertise
nodes.description: Identifying confounders generally requires domain expertise.

nodes.name: Missing confounders can make interpretation untenable
nodes.description: If potential confounders (e.g., social determinants of health, patient preferences) are unavailable in the data, a causal interpretation may be untenable if their influence could flip the conclusions.

nodes.name: Small unmeasured confounders should still be disclosed
nodes.description: Even if unmeasured confounders are believed small in magnitude, they should be acknowledged as a limitation when communicating findings.

nodes.name: Sensitivity analyses provide further assurance
nodes.description: As further assurance, one can employ sensitivity analyses that quantify the magnitude of an unobserved confounder necessary to change the conclusions.

components.description: SUTVA: consistency and non-interference violations, and how ML practitioners without clinical expertise can mishandle them.

nodes.name: SUTVA requires consistency and non-interference
nodes.description: SUTVA requires that all patients receive the same version of treatment (consistency) and that no patient's outcome is affected by others' treatment assignments (non-interference).

nodes.name: Hidden treatment variation causes consistency violations
nodes.description: Consistency violations may arise from hidden variation in the treatment variable, e.g., dose strength.

nodes.name: Treating variation source as a confounder washes out effect
nodes.description: When sources of treatment variation are inadvertently treated as confounders (e.g., dose strength), subsequent adjustment can wash out the treatment effect.

nodes.name: Interference example: nosocomial infection transmission
nodes.description: Interference may occur when treating one patient affects outcomes for others, as in nosocomial infection management, where an ML model might use room ID (predictive of transmission) as a feature.

nodes.name: Non-expert ML practitioners may misclassify these variables
nodes.description: ML practitioners with limited clinical expertise may overlook the causal significance of variables like dose strength or room ID and include them in model development purely because they boost predictive performance.

nodes.name: Correct handling requires distinguishing treatment-definition vs. interference variables
nodes.description: The predictive utility of dose strength suggests it should be incorporated into the treatment definition, whereas the utility of room ID reflects interference rather than treatment, requiring different handling.

nodes.name: Without expertise, predictive associations get mistaken for causal factors
nodes.description: Without domain expertise, researchers risk mistaking predictive associations for sources of treatment effect heterogeneity or genuine causal factors.

components.description: Synthesis of identification-challenges section into a single takeaway.

nodes.name: DAG-first, domain-expert-checked workflow required
nodes.description: It is essential to first define a causal DAG, then examine the data for potential assumption violations using domain expertise and empirical checks.

nodes.name: ML flexibility raises overfitting-to-spurious-signal risk across all three assumptions
nodes.description: The flexibility of ML models increases the risk of overfitting to spurious signals that may obscure violations of overlap, exchangeability, and SUTVA.

nodes.name: Careful collaborative variable/model selection mitigates risk
nodes.description: Careful selection of confounders, treatment/outcome definitions, and associated models in collaboration with domain experts can mitigate assumption-violation risks or quantify their potential impact.

components.description: Covariate selection for modeling: avoiding irrelevant variables and mediators.

nodes.name: Temptation to include all covariates
nodes.description: For ML practitioners it is tempting to incorporate all observed covariates as predictors to adjust for confounding.

nodes.name: Irrelevant variables risk spurious correlation
nodes.description: Irrelevant variables may be spuriously correlated with the outcome.

nodes.name: Mediators lie on the treatment-outcome path
nodes.description: Some variables may be causal mediators — intermediate variables caused by the treatment that influence the outcome, occurring along the DAG path from treatment to outcome.

nodes.name: Adjusting for mediators dilutes treatment effect estimates
nodes.description: Adjusting for mediators dilutes estimates of treatment effects, since the treatment may not get credit for changes in outcomes it caused via the mediator.

nodes.name: Consulting the DAG avoids mediator inclusion
nodes.description: One can avoid including mediators by consulting the DAG and ensuring all predictors are measured before treatment and follow-up.

components.description: Metalearner modeling choices: indirect vs. direct estimators and their robustness trade-offs.

nodes.name: Metalearners plug in arbitrary base models
nodes.description: Metalearners allow users to plug in base models of arbitrary complexity and estimate treatment effects from combinations of the base models' outputs.

nodes.name: Indirect estimators predict outcomes per arm then difference
nodes.description: Indirect estimators (S-learner, T-learner) estimate the outcome under each treatment assignment separately given covariates, then take the difference.

nodes.name: Indirect estimators are fragile to base-model error
nodes.description: Because the treatment effect is the difference between two separate predictions, errors in either prediction can be magnified and distort the final estimate.

nodes.name: Regularization can flatten outcome estimates and conceal heterogeneity
nodes.description: In high-dimensional data, model-simplifying techniques like regularization can shrink away treatment heterogeneity, flattening outcome estimates and potentially causing a premature conclusion of no treatment effect.

nodes.name: Direct estimators model treatment effect explicitly
nodes.description: Direct estimators (X-learner, DR-learner, R-learner, double ML, orthogonal statistical learning) use base-model outputs to model the treatment effect directly in a second step, via pseudo-outcomes or residual-based isolation, since the true effect is never directly observed per individual.

nodes.name: Direct methods more robust to base-model error
nodes.description: Although base-model errors can still bias direct methods' estimates, direct methods are often more robust to these errors than indirect methods.

components.description: Synthesis of modeling-choices section into a single takeaway.

nodes.name: DAG consultation reduces irrelevant/mediator inclusion risk
nodes.description: Consulting the causal DAG when choosing covariates reduces the risk of including irrelevant variables and mediators.

nodes.name: Choice of combination method affects estimate quality
nodes.description: The method of combining base model outputs (indirect vs. direct) impacts the quality of treatment effect estimates.

nodes.name: Direct methods preferable when base-model accuracy is a central concern
nodes.description: Indirect methods are attractive for their simplicity, but if the accuracy of base models is a central concern, direct methods may be preferable.

components.description: Evaluation problem: no ground-truth treatment effect, and the surrogate strategies proposed instead.

nodes.name: No true treatment effect for validation
nodes.description: In causal inference only the outcome under the assigned treatment is observed, so there is no 'true' treatment effect available for held-out validation as in standard supervised ML.

nodes.name: Standard ML test-set paradigm does not apply
nodes.description: Because there is no ground-truth treatment effect, the standard ML paradigm of comparing predicted to observed outcomes on a held-out test set does not apply to causal effect evaluation.

nodes.name: Global null analysis proposed
nodes.description: One strategy is a global null analysis using a synthetic treatment with no true effect, allowing estimated effects to be directly evaluated similarly to supervised ML since the expected effect is zero.

nodes.name: Negative control / plasmode simulation as complements
nodes.description: To complement a global null analysis, one can perform a negative control analysis (a treatment with no effect per expert knowledge) or plasmode simulation when feasible.

nodes.name: Cross-modeling-approach stability as a second strategy
nodes.description: Another strategy is comparing estimates across different modeling approaches and assessing whether sign and magnitude are stable, since each approach encodes different assumptions.

nodes.name: Stability builds confidence but doesn't replace RCTs
nodes.description: Stability across modeling approaches builds confidence in results but these analyses do not supersede evaluation through RCTs or grounding in real-world causal mechanisms.

components.description: Synthesis of evaluation section: treat causal ML outputs as hypotheses, not findings.

nodes.name: Gold-standard validation generally infeasible
nodes.description: Gold-standard validation is generally infeasible in observational causal inference.

nodes.name: Results should be treated as hypotheses, not definitive findings
nodes.description: Causal ML results from observational data should be treated as causal hypotheses rather than definitive findings.

nodes.name: Hypotheses can guide RCT prioritization or mechanistic evaluation
nodes.description: These hypotheses can then be prioritized for testing in RCTs or evaluated against plausible physiological or biological mechanisms.

components.description: Overall conclusion: toward responsible use, and the proposed roadmap.

nodes.name: Unjustified assumptions/choices risk misleading conclusions
nodes.description: Without well-justified causal assumptions and ML modeling choices, analyses may yield conclusions that are misleading.

nodes.name: Roadmap proposed organizing recommendations
nodes.description: A roadmap is proposed that organizes recommendations for using causal ML in observational data into questions addressing causal assumptions, modeling, and evaluation.

nodes.name: Roadmap is a non-exhaustive foundation for interdisciplinary teams
nodes.description: Although not exhaustive, the roadmap offers a foundation for interdisciplinary teams to ground their causal ML analyses.

isolated_nodes.name: Causal ML adapts standard ML techniques for causal inference
isolated_nodes.description: Regardless of the use case (population-level trends or personalized treatment-effect prediction), the field of causal ML adapts standard ML techniques for causal inference.

isolated_nodes.name: Paper scopes to binary treatment/outcome
isolated_nodes.description: The paper considers the setting of a binary treatment and outcome to lay the foundation for more complex analyses (e.g., multiple treatments), as a deliberate scoping choice.
